lessons.title: Claim and reason
lessons.tip: A claim is what you want people to accept: “Schools should start later.” A reason answers “why?”: “because teenagers need more sleep.” A good argument joins them with “because.” A claim without a reason is only an opinion.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Choose strong evidence
lessons.tip: Evidence is a fact, an example, a number or an expert’s view that supports a reason. Strong evidence is specific, true and connected to the claim. Weak evidence is vague (“everyone knows”), only personal (“my cousin did this”) or about something else.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Order an argument
lessons.tip: A clear argument has four parts: claim, reason, evidence and conclusion. Start with the claim, say why, prove it, and finish by repeating the claim in a stronger way. Signpost each step with words like “first,” “for example” and “therefore.”
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Phrases for arguing
lessons.tip: Good speakers use set phrases. To give an opinion: “In my opinion…,” “I believe…” To add a point: “Moreover…,” “Also…” To give an example: “For instance…” To contrast: “On the other hand…,” “However…” To conclude: “In conclusion…,” “To sum up…”

lessons.title: A polite rebuttal
lessons.tip: A rebuttal answers another person’s argument. First show you listened: “I see your point.” Then say where you disagree: “However, …” or “I’m not sure that’s true, because …” Attack the argument, not the person.
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Straw man and personal attack
lessons.tip: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument look stronger than it is. A straw man changes someone’s argument into a weaker one and attacks that. An ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument. Spot them and name them calmly.

lessons.title: False dilemma and slippery slope
lessons.tip: A false dilemma says there are only two choices when there are more: “Either we ban cars or the city dies.” A slippery slope says one small step will lead to a disaster without proof: “If we allow short breaks, soon nobody will work.” Ask: Are there other choices? Is each step really certain?
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Weigh two arguments

lessons.title: Check your sources
lessons.tip: Before you use a fact, ask four questions: Who wrote it? Do they know the subject? Is it recent? Do they gain something if you believe it? A source that gains from your belief is not worthless, but you should look for a second source. Say it plainly: “This comes from the company that sells the product, so I checked another report.”
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Numbers that mislead
lessons.tip: Numbers feel strong, but they can mislead. A “50 percent rise” from 2 cases to 3 cases is small in real life. Ask how big the group was and how people were chosen. A percentage point is a different thing from a percent: a rise from 10 percent to 15 percent is 5 percentage points, or a 50 percent rise. Always ask: compared with what?

Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Cause or coincidence?
lessons.tip: Two things can happen together without one causing the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause sunburn. A third factor, hot weather, explains both. When you read “X leads to Y,” ask whether something else could explain both, and whether X came first. Use careful words: “is linked to” is safer than “causes.”
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Examples and analogies
lessons.tip: One example is a story, not proof. Three examples help, but a fair sample helps more. An analogy compares two situations: “Banning phones is like banning pencils.” It is strong only if the two situations are alike in the way that matters. Test it: In what way are they alike, and in what important way are they different?
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (public-domain translations): reason and evidence as a basis for persuasion
Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, and Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett (concepts only; no text copied)

lessons.title: Warrants and hidden assumptions
lessons.tip: Every argument rests on a link between its grounds and its claim. Toulmin called this link the warrant. It is often unstated: “The air is unsafe, so the authority must act” assumes that authorities are responsible for health. A warrant can be attacked even when the grounds are true. Name it, test it, and add a qualifier when you cannot be certain: “probably,” “in most cases,” “unless…”

lessons.title: Burden of proof
lessons.tip: The burden of proof is the duty to support a claim. In most debates the side proposing a change must show why it is needed; the status quo is presumed acceptable until shown otherwise. Shifting the burden unfairly is a trick: “Prove that it will not work” demands proof of a negative. Say plainly who must prove what: “The proposal carries the burden of showing that the benefits exceed the costs.”

Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett, and the principle of charity (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Charity and the strongest version
lessons.tip: The principle of charity says: interpret an opponent’s argument in the strongest reasonable way before you answer it. If you defeat a weak version, you have defeated nothing. State their case so well that they would say, “Yes, that is what I meant.” This is steelmanning. Then answer the strongest point. Charity also protects you: it stops you from winning a point that does not matter.

Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett, and the principle of charity (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Find the crux
lessons.tip: Many debates stall because the sides argue about different things. The crux is the point where the disagreement actually lies. lessons.title: Frames and reframes
lessons.tip: A frame is the way an issue is described, and it shapes what seems reasonable. “Tax relief” suggests a burden; “public investment” suggests a benefit. Notice the frame in an argument and ask whether it is fair. You can reframe by describing the same facts in terms of different values: not “a ban on cars” but “streets for people.” Use frames honestly: a fair frame is one you could defend to the other side.

lessons.title: Layered rebuttal
lessons.tip: A strong rebuttal has layers. First label the point you answer: “On their second argument…” Then state the claim of your answer, give your reason and show the impact: “…it does not follow, because the sample was small, so the policy rests on weak evidence.” Where possible, offer more than one layer: your answer is true, and even if it were not, the effect is small. lessons.title: Argue under uncertainty
lessons.tip: Often nobody knows what will happen. Compare options by probability (how likely), magnitude (how big) and reversibility (can it be undone?). A small chance of a huge, permanent harm can outweigh a likely small gain. Be precise about uncertainty: “likely,” “plausible” and “possible” are not the same. Avoid false certainty on either side: “It will certainly work” and “It could never work” both need proof.
sources: Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (concepts only: claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal; no text copied)
Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett, and the principle of charity (concepts only; original wording)

lessons.title: Weigh and close
lessons.tip: In a closing speech, do not repeat everything. Identify the two or three issues that decide the debate, say who won each and why, and explain why those issues outweigh the rest. This is called weighing or impact comparison: “Even if they win the cost point, our point concerns lives, which matters more.” Compare size, likelihood and who is affected. End with a clear, short statement of why your side should win.
sources: Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (concepts only: claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal; no text copied)
Rapoport’s rules as described by Dennett, and the principle of charity (concepts only; original wording)
